entry.title: Mistral launches Voxtral 3 voice agent SDK with real-time multilingual transcription, expressive speech synthesis, and deep tool integration for EU-hosted or self-deployed use [ * ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Mistral has introduced Voxtral 3, a voice agent SDK and speech model suite designed for real-time, multi-step conversations in over 50 languages. It combines accurate speech-to-text transcription, natural text-to-speech with emotional adaptability, and integrated tool calling to enable seamless workflow automation for contact centers, virtual assistants, and hands-free copilots. Voxtral 3 is available via Mistral's EU-hosted API or for self-deployment, allowing organizations to maintain data sovereignty and control over audio processing and retention. The Voxtral 3 family includes state-of-the-art transcription models that support diarization and context biasing, outperforming competitors like Whisper and Gemini 3.5 Transcribe. Its text-to-speech models adapt voice emotion, pace, and emphasis based on conversational context across 35+ languages and 50+ dialects. The SDK enables agents to listen, reason, interact with business systems, and execute multi-step tasks during live conversations. A Pro Voice feature offers advanced voice adaptation using just 30 minutes of audio to replicate a speaker's distinctive style and emotional range.

entry.title: DeepSeek releases DeepInfer, a high-performance inference framework for DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash models supporting NVIDIA SM100 GPUs and Huawei Ascend 950 NPUs [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: DeepSeek has open-sourced DeepInfer, a high-performance inference framework designed for large-scale production services using DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash models. The framework supports optimized kernels, parallelism, asynchronous scheduling, deterministic sampling, and structured outputs, targeting NVIDIA SM100 GPUs and Huawei Ascend 950 NPUs. DeepInfer requires Linux, GCC 13.0 or higher, Python 3.12, and CUDA 13 or CANN 9.2 depending on the hardware. It provides offline inference capabilities with features like confidence-scheduled verification and batch-invariant inference. The release does not include a complete inference service, as components like KV cache systems and load balancing are needed separately.

entry.title: Alibaba raises DeepSeek V4 Flash 0731 output prices by 230%, input costs more than double overnight [ * ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Alibaba increased the output price of its DeepSeek V4 Flash 0731 model from $0.40 to $1.32 per million tokens, a 230% rise, while input costs rose from $0.20 to $0.44 per million tokens. This sudden price hike reflects a broader trend of AI labs raising inference costs, impacting developers who rely on subsidized compute pricing. Other providers like Mistral and Alibaba's Qwen3.6 model also raised prices significantly, while Zhipu AI reduced prices on one model by 85%. The shift signals the end of heavily subsidized AI compute, urging builders to optimize token usage and caching to maintain profitability.

entry.title: Researchers propose TTCS, a co-evolving test-time training framework that synthesizes curricula to improve large language models' reasoning on challenging tasks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers introduce TTCS, a test-time training method that simultaneously evolves a question synthesizer and a reasoning solver from the same pretrained model. The synthesizer generates progressively harder question variants tailored to the solver's current ability, while the solver updates itself using self-consistency rewards from multiple responses on both original and synthetic questions. This approach addresses difficulties in existing methods caused by overly hard test questions and limited test set sizes, which hinder stable model adaptation. Experiments demonstrate that TTCS enhances reasoning performance on challenging mathematical benchmarks and general-domain tasks across different large language model backbones. The framework offers a scalable way to dynamically construct test-time curricula for self-improving models, with code and implementation details made publicly available.

entry.title: WeAct introduces dynamic weight switching via capability-specific LoRA adapters as agent actions, improving Qwen3-32B accuracy by 6.2% over full fine-tuning and enabling modular continual adaptation [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: WeAct proposes a method for long-horizon agents to dynamically switch between capability-specific LoRA adapters during execution, addressing catastrophic forgetting by freezing the backbone and treating adapter selection as internal agent actions. This approach allows on-demand composition of capabilities within a shared context, improving performance across eight benchmarks. In experiments with the Qwen3-32B model, WeAct achieved a 6.2% accuracy improvement compared to full fine-tuning and a 27.5% gain over the strongest static LoRA-merging method, while using less compute. The method also supports modular continual adaptation by adding or updating adapters without altering the backbone or other adapters, enhancing agent flexibility and report quality.

entry.title: OpenAI improves AI coding models for low-resource languages like COBOL, Fortran, and Visual Basic with higher accuracy and lower cost in software building and migration tasks [ * ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: OpenAI has enhanced its AI models to better support programming in low-resource languages such as COBOL, Fortran, and Visual Basic, which are critical for banking, weather forecasting, and other essential services. The improvements focus on building new software and migrating existing code while preserving functionality, addressing challenges like limited documentation and legacy code maintenance. The company developed two evaluations: MultiLangBench, which tests building a SQLite-compatible database engine across 20 languages, and a COBOL migration evaluation that assesses code translation accuracy. The latest models, including GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol, show significant gains in accuracy and cost efficiency compared to previous versions, with GPT-6 Astra achieving an 87.4% average pass rate on MultiLangBench and GPT-6.1 Sol reaching up to 97.9% accuracy in COBOL migration tasks. These advancements aim to help developers maintain and modernize software in languages that underpin vital infrastructure, with OpenAI releasing the MultiLangBench evaluation setup and test suite publicly to support further development and assessment.

entry.title: Researchers introduce VibeTraining-Bench to evaluate recursive self-improvement via co-design of training data, trainers, and inference harnesses across diverse AI tasks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: VibeTraining-Bench is a new benchmark designed to assess AI agents' ability to iteratively improve system performance by jointly optimizing training data, trainers, and inference harnesses, a process termed cross-component co-design. The benchmark covers tasks in terminal operation, software engineering, multi-turn tool use, and mathematical reasoning, with agents starting from identical initial systems and refining components under fixed resource constraints. Safeguards such as test data isolation and network restrictions are implemented to prevent reward hacking. Evaluation results demonstrate that advanced research agents can significantly enhance target agent systems; for instance, GPT-6-Astra improved performance on the SWE-bench Verified task from 32.9% to 53.7%, nearing the 55.4% achieved by a human-developed instruct model. Despite these gains, the study notes ongoing challenges in achieving cumulative improvements through iterative co-design. The authors aim for VibeTraining-Bench to serve as a unified platform to advance recursive self-improvement and deepen understanding of cross-component optimization in AI systems, with code and data publicly available.

entry.title: Researchers introduce a counterfactual evaluation framework separating targets and updates in LLM-proposed repair actions, tested on traffic assignment and database repair tasks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers propose a counterfactual evaluation framework that separates the selection of records (targets) from the applied changes (updates) in repair actions suggested by large language models (LLMs). The framework measures the effects of correcting or retaining each component by combining proposed and reference targets and updates in four executions. It was evaluated on two tasks: traffic assignment, where affected demand is identified from road counts, and database repair, where affected rows are identified from aggregate reports, using injected faults and recovery rates to assess performance. The study found that the value of a proposed update depends on the targets it is paired with; missed targets can hide useful updates, while excess targets may make milder updates more effective than reference corrections. In traffic experiments, retaining the proposed update on reference targets achieved 79.4% of the reference loss reduction, outperforming tuning update strength on proposed targets. In database experiments, replacing updates worsened some actions, especially those selecting unaffected records, with variation across models. A component-reuse study combining target-update pairings from two proposals improved the mean held-out recovery rate compared to selecting between original proposals.

entry.title: Researchers model service-induced GPU memory congestion in large language model serving, identifying instability and throughput loss mechanisms under high concurrency [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Large language model (LLM) serving accumulates persistent GPU memory usage as each request's key-value cache grows with generated tokens, leading to endogenous memory pressure under high concurrency. When memory capacity is exceeded, active requests are evicted and restarted, causing wasted computation and reduced throughput. Researchers developed a discrete-time dynamical model capturing admission, memory growth, and eviction under continuous batching, revealing that homogeneous workloads tend toward unstable eviction-free equilibria and converge to stable limit cycles with up to 50% throughput loss. For heterogeneous workloads, the study proves a stability criterion and shows that workload diversity can desynchronize completions and stabilize memory-constrained serving. The findings identify service-induced congestion as a structural instability and propose scheduling design principles to sustain high throughput in memory-limited LLM inference environments.

entry.title: Researchers propose BridgeCast, a Transformer-based probabilistic model using conditional flow matching to correct biases in ocean wave forecasts by transforming them into reanalysis-like fields with exogenous atmospheric variables [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: BridgeCast is a physics-AI hybrid model designed to improve ocean wave forecasting by correcting systematic biases in physics-based models. It treats physical model forecasts as corrupted observations and uses a continuous-time generative process to align their distribution with reanalysis data, leveraging a Transformer architecture for spatiotemporal modeling and incorporating external atmospheric variables. The model supports flexible inference through ordinary and stochastic differential equations and has been tested extensively on real-world datasets, consistently outperforming state-of-the-art baselines across different regions and forecast lead times. This approach aims to enhance maritime safety, offshore operations, and coastal resilience by providing more accurate wave forecasts.

entry.title: Researchers introduce reverse-geocoding-based location encoders that incorporate administrative boundaries, improving geospatial prediction tasks with a new RevGeoRQ architecture [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers have developed a method to train location encoders that explicitly incorporate administrative boundaries and place names by using reverse-geocoded text as a self-supervised signal. This approach enhances existing location encoder architectures and improves their performance on downstream geospatial tasks. The team also introduced RevGeoRQ, a custom architecture optimized for reverse-geocoding supervision, which outperforms current location encoders on several benchmarks. The method provides more interpretable geographic representations through human-readable reverse-geocoded strings and semantic IDs, with code and model weights planned for release.

entry.title: Muse Glimmer launches 30B-parameter open-source language model with perception encoder for on-device autonomous agentic tasks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Muse Glimmer introduces a 30 billion parameter causal language model designed for autonomous agentic tasks on consumer hardware, integrating multi-step reasoning, tool use, and failure recovery without cloud dependency. The model processes text and image inputs, supports over 100 languages, and is quantized for efficient single-GPU inference. It achieves state-of-the-art performance among similar-sized models on benchmarks for tool use, planning, and task completion. Released under the Apache 2.0 license, Muse Glimmer aims to promote open-source development of capable and safe local AI agents.

entry.title: Stable Signer V3 introduces 4D Deformable Primitive Splatting for high-resolution sign language avatars, improving facial expression, body deformation, and appearance details [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Stable Signer V3 is a new interactive sign language avatar system that uses 4D Deformable Primitive Splatting to overcome limitations in existing avatars, such as restricted facial expressions, inaccurate body deformation specific to individuals, and loss of fine appearance details. The system incorporates Shared Face Primitive Splatting for enhanced expression control, Test-Time Body Primitive Splatting for identity-specific motion fidelity, and Test-Time Tunneling Super-Resolution to recover high-resolution details. These test-time modules are optimized once per signer identity, enabling efficient inference from stored parameters. Evaluations show significant reductions in facial geometry error by 71.4%, body-boundary error by 35.1%, and RGB reconstruction error by 24.2%, while maintaining interactive streaming performance.

entry.title: Researchers propose WSR-Tune, a weight space reparameterization method to preserve safety during fine-tuning of large language models by isolating and freezing safety-critical directions [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Fine-tuning large language models (LLMs) on downstream tasks often compromises their aligned safety behaviors, creating a trade-off between task adaptation and safety preservation. Researchers propose WSR-Tune, a framework that reparameterizes weight matrices to concentrate safety-relevant information into a small subset of directions, which are then frozen during fine-tuning while other directions are updated for task adaptation. This approach reduces interference between safety and task objectives, enabling simultaneous safety retention and improved downstream performance. Experimental results demonstrate that WSR-Tune achieves a better balance between maintaining safety and enhancing task performance compared to existing methods.

entry.title: Alter launches privileged access management platform for multi-user AI agents with per-agent keys, policy enforcement, and audit trails [ * ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Alter has introduced a privileged access management platform designed for AI agents operating on behalf of multiple users. The platform provides each agent with its own identity and scoped credentials, enforces least-privilege policies, keeps credentials private, and maintains a tamper-evident audit trail of all actions. This approach aims to replace shared, over-scoped keys scattered across codebases with a centralized vault and fine-grained access control. The platform integrates with over 140 providers and supports first-class integrations with LangChain, MCP, and AWS. It offers features such as credential vaulting, policy enforcement with default-deny rules, human approval workflows for sensitive calls, and real-time auditing that can be streamed to security information and event management (SIEM) systems. Alter also emphasizes security through encrypted credential storage, fail-closed authorization, and continuous monitoring, aiming to help teams meet customer security reviews and compliance requirements.

entry.title: Navalia framework advances Cowork Agents with verifiable task synthesis and long-horizon post-training, improving financial analysis and general office task performance [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Navalia is a new framework designed to enhance Cowork Agents-large language model agents capable of autonomous planning and complex task execution-by combining verifiable task synthesis with long-horizon post-training. It uses corporate financial reports to select evidence and build computation chains for analytical tasks, verified through independent LLM review and programmatic checks. The verified tasks support supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning to improve long-horizon task execution. Initialized from the Qwen3.6-35B-A3B model, Navalia shows consistent performance gains across five benchmarks including OfficeQA Pro and Finance Agent Benchmark. The framework improves evidence integration, tool use, and task execution capabilities, and generalizes to broader Cowork settings beyond financial analysis, such as general office tasks.

entry.title: Researchers propose autonomous construction method using large language model and reinforcement learning to control mobile cranes and update progress with ChatGPT 5 [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Researchers have developed an autonomous construction approach combining a large language model and reinforcement learning to improve building efficiency amid rising housing demand. The method uses an enhanced soft actor-critic reinforcement learning algorithm to plan mobile crane actions, supported by robot kinematics and control algorithms to execute tasks accurately. A customized embedding model extracts relevant environmental information, while ChatGPT 5 updates construction progress, provides safety information, and generates reports. The approach was validated through full-scale retaining wall construction experiments, demonstrating its feasibility for smart construction applications.

entry.title: Researchers propose multi-objective reinforcement learning method for LLM-based RTL circuit generation optimizing diverse Pareto-optimal solutions in power, performance, and area [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Researchers have developed a new learning method that uses large language models (LLMs) to generate RTL circuits optimized for multiple objectives-power, performance, and area-simultaneously. Unlike previous approaches that combine these objectives into a single reward, this method aims to produce a diverse set of Pareto-optimal circuits, allowing designers to select preferred trade-offs based on specific product requirements. The approach includes a generation-based training pipeline and a reward function based on Hypervolume Contribution to measure each circuit's contribution to the Pareto front. Evaluation on the RTLLM v2 benchmark demonstrated that this method improves relative Hypervolume by 13.3 percentage points over a baseline without PPA optimization and by 14.4 percentage points over single-objective reinforcement learning, while also enhancing circuit diversity. This advancement supports more flexible and efficient RTL circuit design by providing a broader range of high-quality candidate solutions.

entry.title: MedPAO-Assist launches edge-deployable AI for structured radiology reports using small language models on standard laptop CPUs [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: MedPAO-Assist is an agentic AI framework designed to generate structured radiology reports from dictation and voice commands, operating offline with about 3.3 GB RAM and 31 seconds latency on a standard laptop CPU. It supports four imaging modalities-Chest X-ray, Chest CT, Abdomen CT, and Brain MRI-and uses a multi-agent Extract-Ground-Generate architecture with a small 0.6 billion parameter language model, enabling a fully voice-driven, no-keyboard workflow without internet connectivity or external APIs. The system performs concept extraction, SNOMED-CT ontology grounding, and structured report generation, followed by a speech-driven human-in-the-loop correction phase. Hardware profiling and individual pipeline evaluations demonstrate its feasibility for real-time clinical deployment on CPU-only devices, addressing data privacy and offline operation challenges common in radiology workflows.

entry.title: DataPraxis introduces a verified workspace evolution framework to scale analytics task synthesis and releases DataPraxis-5K dataset with 5,000 verified trajectories for training large models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: DataPraxis presents a new framework for synthesizing analytics tasks through verified workspace evolution, which progressively enriches workspaces with validated findings to uncover deeper analytical questions. This approach addresses limitations in generating tasks directly from raw data by verifying results during workspace evolution and task assembly. The team released DataPraxis-5K, a dataset of 5,000 verified analytic trajectories across diverse domains and output formats, used to train large models DataPraxis-27B and DataPraxis-35B-A3B. DataPraxis-27B achieves competitive performance on benchmarks like DABStep and JobBench, matching or surpassing models such as GLM-5.2. The dataset is publicly available on Hugging Face.

entry.title: Industrial Agentic AI: LLM-Driven New-Generation Agents for Smart Manufacturing [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2610.26941v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are enabling agents to move beyond predefined workflows toward autonomous planning and execution, creating new opportunities for smart manufacturing. However, dynamic environments, complex physical constraints, and stringent reliability requirements hinder the direct deployment of general-purpose agents in smart manufacturing. This article presents a systematic overview of LLM-driven industrial agents. First, we analyze five key challenges and discuss the concept and core characteristics of industrial agents. We then establish a unified taxonomy covering application scenarios, embodiment forms, and five capability levels. Next, we propose a four-layer system architecture and detail its core modules and operational mechanisms for closed-loop task execution. Finally, we review representative applications across the industrial lifecycle and outline future research directions. This article provides a structured reference for the design, development, and application of industrial agents.

entry.title: Fix, Not Just Resample: Bounded Compiler-Guided Repair in Lean 4 [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2610.26942v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Automated theorem provers often rely on sampling language models, but proof assistants like Lean reject each failed step with a precise error message --- information that pure sampling discards. To overcome this, we introduce a bounded, online step-level repair module. Our search samples $K$ candidate tactics at each step and repairs a failed tactic at most $R$ times. Instead of discarding failed tactics, we feed the compiler's error message to a pretrained repair model to fix individual rejected steps in place. This approach improves the solve rate over a sampling-only baseline across all tested candidate budgets ($K \in \{1,3,5,8\}$), achieving up to a $32\%$ relative gain and solving $82$ additional theorems on a $1{,}990$-theorem subset of the LeanDojo benchmark. Repair is not free: it trades extra runtime for reachable proofs. But the trade is predictable: repair pays most when sampling is constrained; its return is front-loaded, with the first repair attempt capturing $84\text{--}96\%$ of the total gain; and the gain comes almost entirely from shallow tactic-execution failures rather than structural errors such as type mismatches. This targeted repair successfully replicates on a second benchmark (Lean Workbook), nearly doubling the solve rate with zero regressions.

entry.title: MAMath-Bench: Process-Aware and Robust Evaluation of Multimodal Multi-Agent Mathematical Reasoning [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2610.26943v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Mathematical reasoning is a fundamental capability for educational applications of Large Language Models (LLMs), where reliable problem solving requires not only correct answers but also coherent and verifiable reasoning processes. Multi-agent systems (MASs) have shown growing potential in this domain by leveraging collaboration and verification among multiple LLM agents. However, existing evaluations primarily focus on the correctness of final answers in text-only settings, offering limited insight into multimodal reasoning capabilities, the reliability of intermediate reasoning steps, and robustness against reasoning errors. To address these limitations, we introduce MAMath-Bench, a process-aware benchmark designed to evaluate the multimodal mathematical reasoning capabilities of MASs. MAMath-Bench comprises 1,003 problems spanning 11 mathematical categories, multiple difficulty levels, and several modalities, including text, images, and audio. It features fine-grained milestone annotations to evaluate systems across three dimensions: problem-solving correctness, reasoning-process reliability, and robustness to adversarial reasoning-chain perturbations. Our evaluation yields three key findings. First, multi-agent collaboration does not consistently improve final-answer accuracy over strong single LLMs. Second, collaboration can substantially enhance the coverage of intermediate reasoning, but such gains may come at the cost of increased reasoning redundancy. Third, current systems remain vulnerable to adversarial reasoning errors, particularly those involving subtle structural perturbations. The dataset is available at https://github.com/mira-ai-lab/AgentMath.

entry.title: LightCRS: Lightweight Multi-Domain Conversational Recommendation System [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2610.26948v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Conversational recommender systems have recently adopted vision-language models to match user dialogue intents with multimodal product information. However, extending these methods to many product domains faces a dilemma: deploying a separately adapted VLM per domain scales cost linearly with the number of domains and requires routing each dialogue to the right model, while naively merging all domains into a single VLM degrades accuracy because product characteristics vary widely across categories. We propose LightCRS, a lightweight, query-conditioned framework for unified multi-domain multimodal conversational recommendation. LightCRS precomputes multimodal product representations once offline with frozen encoders. Online, a compact 5.3M-parameter module fuses this evidence for each dialogue via query-conditioned cross-attention, whose parameters are shared across all domains, and compares candidates jointly with an inter-candidate Transformer. To enable rigorous evaluation, we construct MM-R2A-25, a 25-domain benchmark pairing natural Reddit recommendation-seeking conversations with Amazon product listings. LightCRS achieves state-of-the-art average HR@1, NDCG@5, and MRR, improving HR@1 by 35.4\% over the strongest baseline while reducing per-query latency by 266 times. Joint multi-domain training itself improves HR@1 by 15.2\% over separately trained single-domain models.

entry.title: When Planning Problems Become Hard for LLMs: Separating Structural Complexity from Semantic Interpretability [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2610.26964v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) struggle with classical planning, but benchmarks rarely distinguish structural difficulty from the difficulty of interpreting symbolic vocabulary. We examine seven STRIPS domains with BFS-optimal plan lengths. For predicting structural difficulty without solving an instance, the zero-training delete-relaxation heuristic $h_{\mathrm{add}}$ outperforms learned alternatives on held-out domains (mean Spearman $|\rho|=0.931$), including ridge regression ($0.707$), object count ($0.657$), and the episodic retrieval architecture ARC ($0.400$). ARC also fails to outperform a linear model using the same features. To isolate semantic effects, we progressively rename predicates while preserving states, transitions, and optimal plans. Valid LLM planning success drops from $67.5\%$ to $40.0\%$ between $0\%$ and $100\%$ renaming, while refusals remain at $0\%$. An LLM supplied with ARC's conditioning information predicts difficulty in context better than trained ARC (mean $|\rho|=0.826$). Hybrid routing between an LLM and a symbolic planner depends more on calibration to the target LLM's outcomes than on the structural score selected. Thus, established symbolic heuristics already estimate structural difficulty well; improving hybrid planning requires modeling LLM behavior sensitive to predicate semantics rather than developing more structural predictors.

entry.title: SPEM: Structure-Aware Procedural Memory for Efficient Skill Use in LLM Agents [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2610.26995v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLM-based agents increasingly rely on reusable skills. However, scaling skill libraries makes efficient and accurate skill use difficult. Full skill loading incurs high token and runtime overhead. In contrast, flat semantic retrieval treats skills as independent text entries, ignoring dependencies, execution order, state transitions, and data flow constraints. We propose SPEM, a lightweight structure-aware procedural memory framework for efficient skill use in LLM-based agents. SPEM maintains Atomic Skill Memory for individual skills and Skill-DAG Memory for reusable compositions derived from successful executions. For a new task, SPEM reuses high-confidence Skill-DAG templates when available. Otherwise, it retrieves atomic skills and invokes Skill-GNN for state- and structure-aware skill selection. Successful executions are written back as new Skill-DAGs, allowing procedural memory to accumulate over time. Experiments on ALFWorld and SkillsBench show that SPEM achieves the best overall effectiveness--efficiency trade-off, reaching 87.1% ALFWorld success and 38.38% SkillsBench reward while reducing token and runtime costs against strong baselines.

entry.title: Does Multi-Agent Collaboration Reduce Hallucination in Clinical Tasks? [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2610.27027v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multi-agent LLM systems improve performance on clinical tasks, and that improvement is often read as evidence of a more trustworthy system. However, the two are not the same claim. A clinician acts on the stated reasoning and not only on the conclusion, so whether collaboration reduces hallucination, and what decides when it does, has to be measured in the reasoning too. Yet most evaluations score only the final answer. We evaluate four systems (a single-LLM baseline and three multi-agent topologies) across four models and three clinical tasks, scoring hallucination, under a factuality and faithfulness taxonomy, inside the rationale each system generates and reporting it alongside the task metric. We report that collaboration buys task performance but not lower hallucination as a rule, and no topology is reliably better than another. The effect differs by model: of the $36$ model--system--task comparisons, $12$ are large enough to resolve --- four decreases and eight increases, with no model on both sides. What sets the level, and the direction of any change, is the model rather than the topology or the number of agents. A self-correction experiment is consistent with this: shown its own flagged errors, every model except Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct reduces hallucination; the one model for which collaboration lowers hallucination gains the most, and Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct, the model whose hallucination it amplifies most, does not reduce its hallucination at all. We find that collaboration redistributes what its models can already do; it does not supply what they cannot.

entry.title: Teaching AI Agent to Play Poker Strategically Through Preference Optimization [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2610.27028v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A poker agent can make a legal move and still make a strategically poor one. We ask whether compact AI agents can exhibit strategic behavior under hidden information and whether preference optimization can improve beyond static and zero-shot policies. We first evaluate a static baseline and three frozen language models: SmallThinker, Qwen3, and Gemma-3 whose performance varies substantially between exact-game and six-player evaluation. We therefore propose Strategic Preference Optimization with KL-anchored Equilibrium (SPOKE), combining teacher-relative value penalties, policy anchoring, risk constraints, and structured rationale supervision, and compare it with SFT, DPO, GRPO, and GSPO. Across three runs of a SmallThinker-4B-A0.6B policy, SPOKE achieves the lowest mean exploitability in Kuhn (0.213) and Leduc (1.081) and the highest six-max top-1 agreement (0.775), while maintaining teacher KL comparable to SFT (0.522 vs 0.523). These results provide preliminary evidence that strategic preference optimization can improve strategic quality while preserving teacher-consistent behavior.

entry.title: M-Plan: Comprehensive Planning For LLM Agents with Memory Arrangement [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2610.27032v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language model (LLM)-based agents have recently demonstrated outstanding performance in single-turn tasks, yet they continue to struggle with long-horizon tasks, particularly in environments without prior training. A key limitation of single LLMs is their difficulty in processing long contexts, which stems from weaknesses in continuous decision-making and reasoning capabilities. Although existing multi-agent systems (MAS) equipped with long-term memory bases can partially address this gap, they mostly rely on knowledge reuse or summarization, an approach that is often constrained by directly retrieval without any adaptation for the current task, while the retrieved memory may contain much history noises waiting to be preprocessed. In contrast, MAS characterized by task-specific guidance often lack long-term memory specifically designed for the guidance. To address these challenges, we propose M-Plan, a closed-loop MAS framework that integrates long-term and short-term memory. By combining global-local and past-current guidance, M-Plan enhances agents' performance on multi-turn tasks while maintaining a plug-and-play design. During task execution, agents receive task-specific milestones and insights, and are provided with local hints only when confusion arises, which form global-local guidance together. These guidance generation and utilization construct the short-term memory as well. After task completion, relevant information about the current task is optimized or reorganized before being sent to the long-term memory storage for future retrieval. The designments mentioned above build a comprehensive framework different from other individual long-term or short-term memory works. Extensive experiments on multi-turn tasks including ALFWorld, Webshop, and PDDL across diverse models demonstrate that M-Plan outperforms multiple baseline methods in both accuracy and efficiency.

entry.title: Physical AI: Concepts, Techniques, and Challenges [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2610.27045v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In recent years, physical artificial intelligence (physical AI) has experienced rapid development, capturing significant attention in academia and industry. However, the field has yet to reach consensus on its definition, technical landscape, and core challenges. To address this gap, this monograph seeks to define physical AI, present its technical landscape, and examine each key technical subfield in depth. In doing so, it establishes a unified framework for Physical AI: artificial systems that perceive, model, and act upon the physical world through continuous feedback under real-world constraints. Further, this monograph distinguishes physical AI from conventional digital AI, embodied AI, cyber-physical systems, and digital twins. It develops the foundations of physical AI across physics, control, cognition, learning, and reasoning. It reviews key methodologies, including multimodal perception, physical data and simulation, world models, embodied foundation models, motor-control systems, multi-agent coordination, and hardware-software co-design. Furthermore, it examines applications spanning robotics, manufacturing, infrastructure, scientific experimentation, and autonomous services. Particular attention is given to sim-to-real transfer, reliability, real-time execution, evaluation, safety, governance, and long-term deployment. By connecting perception, prediction, decision-making, action, and adaptation in a closed loop, this monograph identifies the technical challenges and research directions required to advance from narrow automation toward more generalizable physical AI and, ultimately, physical artificial general intelligence (Physical AGI).

entry.title: ReuF2F: Benchmarking Coding Agents on Formalized Undergraduate Research Problems [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2610.27046v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As AI systems begin to resolve open research problems, reliable verification becomes increasingly important. Formal mathematics provides a trusted framework for mathematical reasoning, enabling agents to produce machine-checkable proofs while conducting mathematical exploration. Existing formal mathematics benchmarks often focus on known results or a small set of prominent open problems, which can become difficult to evaluate reliably once solutions are discovered and widely disseminated. Existing evaluation protocols are also not always aligned with how modern coding agents operate. We therefore introduce ReuF2F, a Lean 4 benchmark of 244 formalized open problems drawn from Research Experiences for Undergraduates (REU), spanning entry-level open research problems across a broad range of mathematical subfields. We expect these less prominent open problems, which tend to attract less attention and may remain unsolved for longer, to be better suited for held-out evaluation of end-to-end open problem resolution in Lean. We adopt a standard coding-agent evaluation setting, placing each problem and its logical negation into a Lean project in a Docker container. We also build Leanimum-agent on mini-SWE-agent to provide a unified harness for fair comparisons across models. Our evaluation finds that even the best-performing model resolves only ~40% of the problems, leaving substantial room for improvement on formalized open research problems.

entry.title: A general-purpose System One decision model for clinical records [ * ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2610.27099v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Clinical care, health-system operations and biomedical discovery depend on extracting reliable answers from patient records, yet applying diverse clinical questions across entire populations remains computationally expensive. Here we present Clinical System One (CS1), a 4-billion-parameter decision model for fast, typed judgments from clinical records, along with two agentic harnesses in which CS1 works together with a generalist language model. CS1-4B is trained on 12.4 million questions and answers from 3.6 million patients across a multi-hospital health system, combining structured-data keys, observed outcomes and language-model supervision across clinical notes, diagnostic reports and patient timelines. It answers multiple typed questions in a single forward pass without task-specific retraining, and each answer carries a probability that can route uncertain cases to human review. On 963,408 held-out patients, CS1-4B outperformed open decision models up to 27 billion parameters on 13 of 14 tasks scored independently of its training teacher. Across 21 external data sets, its aggregate performance approached that of the strongest tested 27-billion-parameter model, with 6.4-fold faster inference in a matched workload. Integrating CS1-4B with a language model agent produced cited answers over complete multi-year patient histories and screened a patient population against the eligibility criteria of 17 registered clinical trials, placing four times as many judged-eligible patients among its top 20 candidates as keyword search while using 690-fold fewer language-model tokens than a language model reading every record. These findings support a division of labour in clinical AI, with small decision models performing repeated record reading and generative models formulating questions and synthesizing evidence.

entry.title: Omni-Woodpecker: Hallucination Correction via Evidence-Prior Rebalancing for Omni LLMs [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2610.27103v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recent Omni LLMs (OLLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in joint audio-visual reasoning, yet cross-modal hallucinations remain a major challenge. Existing mitigation methods mainly operate at the output level, overlooking the entanglement of grounding evidence and learned priors within fused representations. To address this issue, we propose Omni-Woodpecker (OWP), a training-free framework that shifts hallucination mitigation from output-level manipulation to conflict-conditioned representation rebalancing. Specifically, OWP first identifies cross-modal conflicts from complementary modality-specific views. It then employs orthogonal decomposition to separate grounding evidence from competing priors within the hidden states. Finally, OWP adaptively rebalances fused representations by suppressing misleading priors and restoring ignored evidence before decoding. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness and strong cross-architecture generalization of OWP. Using Qwen2.5-Omni-7B as the backbone, OWP improves performance by 12.9 and 8.6 points on CMM and AVHBench, respectively, while consistently achieving gains of 0.67-2.25 points across four general OLLM reasoning benchmarks. Furthermore, OWP generalizes effectively to VideoLLaMA2-AV, improving performance by 4.6 and 3.9 points on the same benchmarks. Code is publicly available at https://github.com/ZiiJianLiu/Omni-Woodpecker

entry.title: PROVISO: Provenance-Informed Action Selection for Secure LLM Agents [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2610.27115v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLM agents act on the external world through tools and third-party skills, so a single executed action can cause irreversible harm. Existing defenses judge a proposed action without tracking whether its content comes from the user or from external sources such as tool outputs, and they judge it in isolation rather than against an available alternative, which forces a trade-off between security and utility. We present PROVISO, a controller that decides which action to commit after the agent proposes an action and before it is executed. PROVISO encodes trusted observations, external observations, the proposed action, and an alternative into provenance-typed memory, relates them through role-specific queries, and commits the action with the highest calibrated value learned from outcomes. On four agent security tasks spanning the agent lifecycle, no baseline exceeds PROVISO in both security and utility. PROVISO improves F1 over the strongest baseline by 13.84 points on SkillsBench and by 7.07 points on ToolSafe, and it reaches 88-99 F1 on three additional skill detection benchmarks.

entry.title: PORA: Learning When More Reasoning Pays Off for LLM Agents [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2610.27119v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLM agents perform tasks over multiple steps and revise their actions based on feedback. As the total reasoning budget is often limited and must support future steps, the agent must choose between short and long reasoning before each action. Longer reasoning may improve the final task outcome by preventing later errors, but it also uses budget capacity that may be needed for future decisions. This creates two challenges: estimating the downstream value of long reasoning and deciding when that value is worth using the remaining budget. We propose Paired Outcome-guided Reasoning Allocation (PORA), which learns this decision by comparing short and long reasoning from the same interaction state. During training, \method{} completes the task twice from each selected state, once with a short reasoning allowance and once with a long allowance, and compares their final quality and total processing to estimate when longer reasoning is valuable. During inference, a controller weighs this estimate against learned prices on remaining-budget pressure and chooses either short or long reasoning without running both alternatives. We evaluate PORA across application, memory, code, retail, and mathematics tasks, achieving strong results across all settings. On BFCL memory, it exceeds the strongest existing method by 17.4--32.9 percentage points. Within the same agent, it matches or exceeds always using long reasoning on code and mathematics with 50.6% fewer actor tokens and 31.2% fewer model requests, respectively.

entry.title: EDMA: Entropy-Driven Multimodal Answering [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2610.27120v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multimodal question answering (MMQA) is based on integrating heterogeneous data sources, selectively leveraging relevant modalities, and ignoring distractors. Existing approaches based on Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) improve performance by splitting the task into intermediate steps, but do not quantify how each modality contributes to reaching the final answer. We argue that quantifying the effect that each modality has on the answering process improves process traceability and final performance. Thus, we propose Entropy-Driven Multimodal Answering (EDMA), which uses logical entropy to formalise multimodal QA as an iterative process of entropy reduction and to quantify the contribution of each modality in distinguishing correct from incorrect candidate answers. This enables the construction of quantifiable answering trajectories, where each step is associated with a measurable entropy reduction. EDMA introduces (i) modality-conditioned partitioning to estimate unimodal entropy reduction, (ii) entropy-driven multimodal fusion to capture complementary information across modalities, and (iii) entropy-based selection of the answering trajectory that minimises the most logical entropy. Evaluated across standard MMQA benchmarks, EDMA outperforms competitive prompting baselines, with average gains of 12.8 F1 and 4.6 LLM-J points over Planning Prompting and 18.6 F1 and 8.3 LLM-J points over Chain-of-Thought. Moreover, EDMA outperforms self-consistency baselines and is competitive with the multi-agent system baseline. Moreover, we show that higher entropy correlates with more false positives and, through controlled trajectory selection, demonstrate that logical entropy serves as an effective, monotonic selector for correct reasoning paths, validating entropy level as a reliable proxy for performance.

entry.title: MoSAIK: Motion Search with Artificial Intelligence in K-space [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2610.27156v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Object: Motion artefacts remain a major limitation of routine two-dimensional T2-weighted turbo spin-echo (TSE) brain MRI, reducing diagnostic confidence and often necessitating repeated acquisitions. MoSAIK (Motion Search with AI in K-space) retrospectively estimates in-plane rigid-body motion directly from standard multi-coil TSE k-space. Without a motion-free reference, external navigators, or additional acquisitions, MoSAIK infers motion from k-space self-consistency violations and incorporates predicted parameters into model-based, motion-aware reconstruction rather than synthesizing corrected images. Materials and Methods: Selected complex coil data were represented as log-magnitude and phase channels. A decoupled convolutional embedding and Transformer encoder estimated phase-encoding-line-indexed rotation and two-dimensional translations. Training used motion-free clinical acquisitions with simulated motion; four held-out subjects were evaluated. Component-wise errors assessed estimation; SSIM and PSNR in silico and entropy focus criterion (EFC) in vivo assessed reconstruction. Results: Motion estimation errors were low for both rotation (MSE $<$ 0.2 deg$^2$) and translation (MSE $<$ 0.2 pixels$^2$), with Pearson correlations of approximately 0.96 and 0.94, respectively. In every in-vivo acquisition, more than 75% of slices showed information gain relative to uncorrected reconstructions. MoSAIK reduced visible artefacts while preserving anatomical detail. Discussion: Transformer-based k-space motion-trajectory estimation enables fast retrospective correction of standard clinical TSE brain MRI.

entry.title: Learned Control Variates for Rare Grid-Outage Estimation at Electric Vehicle Charging Stations [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2610.27159v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Public charging of electric vehicles (EVs) adds a large and synchronized load to the distribution feeders. In most networks, it is rare to overload a feeder at the same time. When it does happen, the consequences can be severe: an overloaded feeder stresses its transformers and can trigger cascading outages across a city. Planners who design for high reliability therefore need to estimate very small outage probabilities. To that end, plain Monte Carlo estimation with an expensive grid simulator can require a prohibitively large number of runs for this task. To reduce the number of runs, we propose a control variate (CV) built from a learned classifier of the outage, trained on cheap observable features such as temperature and load forecasts. We show that for any binary learner, the variance reduction is an explicit function of its recall and false-positive rate. Furthermore, we show that control variate based on a Gaussian proxy of the load loses its effect as outages become rarer, while a learner with non-vanishing precision keeps removing a fixed fraction of the variance even in the extreme rare-event regime. We verify these results in numerical experiments using a feeder-overload simulator across three orders of magnitude of outage probability and obtain that even weak learner with a single feature can remove a quarter of the variance, while a boosted-tree learner is able to remove about 60%. We then apply the estimator to the feeder network of Surabaya, Indonesia, in which the Gaussian load model leaves every feeder three to seven times the one-day-in-ten-years blackout target. At the same simulation budget, planning the reserve with the learned CV and a 95% confidence limit reduces the city-wide blackout days by a third compared with Monte Carlo. These results show that learned control variates can help planners design distribution grids that stay reliable against rare outages.

entry.title: LSA-PAST: Layer-Specific Adaptation and Prototype Transport for Compositional Incremental Learning [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2610.27203v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Class-Incremental Learning (CIL) enables models to recognize new classes over time while retaining prior knowledge, but many real-world problems are compositional, where visual concepts arise from combinations of primitives such as states (i.e., red, shiny) and objects (i.e., shoe, car). Standard CIL methods treat each composition as an independent class, ignoring shared primitives and providing no mechanism to stabilize their representations as new compositions arrive. This causes parameter updates to entangle primitives and induce drift that degrades performance on earlier compositions. Compositional Incremental Learning (composition-IL) formalizes this setting by introducing new state-object compositions across tasks. In this paper, we propose Layer-Specific Adaptation with Prototype-Anchored Adapter-Space Transport (LSA-PAST), a parameter-efficient method tailored to composition-IL. LSA integrates Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) into a frozen ViT with depth-specialized adapters for states, objects, and compositions. PAST then maps past, anchored prototypes into the current adapter space through a rehearsal-free affine transform fit on current-task data, enabling old prototypes to remain compatible with new adapters. Extensive experiments demonstrate that LSA-PAST achieves state-of-the-art (SOA) accuracy-forgetting trade-off performance for composition-IL.

entry.title: Sparse RL Relaxation for LLM Reasoning [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2610.27220v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recent work has explored continuous representations in place of discrete tokens during Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning, often referred to as soft CoT. This is motivated by the idea that a mixture of token embeddings can represent a superposition of multiple reasoning possibilities within a single step. However, it remains challenging to train large language models to realize this potential. Existing work has explored reinforcement learning (RL)-style training for soft CoT. However, these approaches treat soft tokens as actions in a Markov decision process rather than as differentiable intermediate computation steps. Thus, they do not propagate gradients across the soft tokens and miss out on the signal of how the choice of one soft token affects the next. In this paper, we propose a sparse relaxation method for RL (called SpaRLax), which leverages the differentiability of soft-CoT reasoning over time steps and makes training more stable and effective. We adopt an entmax sparsity method that adaptively determines the degree of softness, which truncates long-tail noise at confident steps while retaining multiple plausible candidates when uncertain. Across nine reasoning benchmarks, our method achieves the highest average performance compared with baseline methods. Further analyses validate the effective use of soft-token superposition in our approach, and also demonstrate the contribution of adaptive sparsity in our approach.

entry.title: Magnolia: A Persistent-Memory Agent Framework for Computational Chemistry [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2610.27230v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Chemistry has recently entered a high-data regime as molecular databases from high-throughput platforms or computational studies have become available. Increasing automation within the chemical sciences leads to a more digital and precision chemistry. Dedicated scientific agents are becoming central to guiding the chemist through an ever-increasing amount of data and findings, including negative ones. Here, we introduce Magnolia, a persistent-memory artificial intelligence agent framework that integrates computational protocols, from docking to quantum chemistry, lab notebooks and chat logs relying on large language models (LLMs). It relies on a three-tier memory system: session-level observations are automatically captured and distilled into structured learnings, confirmed and elevated to project-tier entries and, when human-validated, promoted to cross-project rules that actively guide subsequent work and provide direct chemical feedback. We illustrate Magnolia on four case studies: quantum-chemical evaluation of aromatic systems (COMPAS database), molecular dynamics of butane and of modified DNA, and a protein-peptide docking campaign. Across these projects, Magnolia tracked 317 runs and accumulated 116 project-tier entries, from which four cross-project rules were promoted; in controlled replays of four tasks, runs with memory passed the checks that runs without it failed (for example, ten of ten docking-configuration checks, against one to four of ten). By combining automation, reproducibility, and human-in-the-loop control, our Magnolia framework streamlines docking, molecular dynamics and quantum chemistry calculations with direct analysis and LLM-augmented feedback, offering accelerated access to computational (bio)chemistry.

entry.title: EGI-BENCH: An Enterprise General Intelligence Benchmark Suite [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2610.27234v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Enterprise adoption of LLMs in agentic workflows is gated by evaluations that span a wide arc of abilities: CRM operations, heterogeneous-document retrieval, personal data understanding, multi-turn planning, tool use, function calling, long-horizon research, and long-context software engineering. These evaluations live today in separate repositories with divergent runners, dependencies, and scoring conventions, which makes cross-benchmark comparison difficult and obscures what a single aggregate number actually represents. We release EGI-BENCH, a unified LLM agent benchmark suite that consolidates eight enterprise facing agent benchmarks (CRMARENA, HERB, PERSONABENCH, USERBENCH, MCP-UNIVERSE, MCPEVAL, BENCHFORCE, LOCOBENCH) behind a single command-line interface with two runtime-budgeted execution modes. On top of the suite we define the Enterprise General Intelligence (EGI) Score, a six-dimensional framework (M1-M6) whose buckets are populated by fine-grained sub-metrics routed from each benchmark rather than by benchmark-level averages. We describe the suite, the sub-metric routing, and the quick/deep budgets, and report results for fourteen frontier and cost-efficient LLMs spanning the GPT, Claude, and Gemini families under quick mode. Top-line EGI ranges from 39.6 (GPT-4o mini) to 65.6 (gpt-5.5), and no single model dominates every capability axis: gpt-5.5 leads task outcome, planning, and retrieval grounding; Claude Sonnet 4.5 leads tool actioning and safety/abstention; and Claude Haiku 4.5 leads engineering quality. Code is available at https://github.com/SalesforceAIResearch/egi-bench.

entry.title: TxnQA: Benchmarking Analytical Reasoning and Evidence Grounding over Transaction Event Sequences [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2610.27256v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Analyzing merchant transaction histories requires dynamic temporal filtering, entity resolution, and aggregation over irregular event streams--operations poorly captured by static tabular or time-series forecasting benchmarks. We introduce TxnQA, an analytical QA benchmark comprising 27 task families (81 templates) alongside a 5-scenario fraud-risk reasoning suite that evaluates both verdicts and supporting evidence over synthetic, privacy-mitigated transaction data. Ground-truth answers are computed programmatically, and model performance is decomposed into format-following rate (FFR), conditional content accuracy (CA), and end-to-end correctness (E2E). Evaluating prompted proprietary baselines and six LoRA-adapted open-weight models shows that adaptation reliably enforces output schemas but leaves arithmetic bottlenecks: Gemma-4-31B-IT and Qwen3-8B attain E2E scores of 0.867 and 0.816, whereas evaluated MoE checkpoints reach only 0.632-0.713. Furthermore, on the 500-instance fraud suite, verdict accuracy frequently exceeds 80%, yet joint accuracy (requiring exact evidence attribution) collapses to at most ~23%. These findings identify schema compliance, semantic calculation, and evidence attribution as three distinct bottlenecks in transaction-sequence QA.

entry.title: A latent control model for realistic rodent motion [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2610.27279v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The development of embodied models of animal behavior is a major goal of the neuro-AI community. Embodied models will enhance our ability to make direct comparisons between biological and artificial agents. To make such comparisons effective, though, we need embodied models that actually move like animals. Previous work has developed virtual animal bodies and techniques for training realistic motion through imitation. However, to date, there is no system for embodied animal modeling that produces natural movements both during trained goal-directed behavior, and during exploration driven by random generation. Here, we introduce Simulated Control via Augmented Motor Priors for Embodied Reinforcement learning (SCAMPER), a system for training an embodied virtual rat model, enabling natural movements during both goal-directed behavior and random exploration. SCAMPER uses a variational architecture with two distinct priors, a motion prior for control and a behavior prior for exploration. We show that combining both of these priors allows SCAMPER to generate realistic behavior during exploration and exploit the task structure effectively. SCAMPER can also learn from sparse rewards as a result of the diverse movements induced by the behavior prior, allowing the system to model realistic sparse-reward tasks from experimental neuroscience. Altogether, SCAMPER provides the neuro-AI community with an effective new system for training embodied models of rodents on realistic tasks.

entry.title: TEX: Test-Time Scaling Testing Agents via Execution-based Cross-Validation [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2610.27290v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Test-case generation is critical but remains challenging for language models. Existing test-time scaling methods either isolate candidates or aggregate traces, which do not scale to long-horizon tasks. We present TEX, a collaborative test-time scaling framework based on execution-driven cross-validation. TEX parallelizes agents to generate tests and patches, cross-executing each test against every patch to form a $K \times K$ feedback matrix. Agents use their matrix slices for refinement, enabling objective validation without verbose trace sharing. On SWT-Bench Verified, TEX achieves 86.4%, establishing a new state-of-the-art and improving +9.0% over single-agent baselines. Moreover, even random selection from TEX outputs (84.4%) surpasses the previous SOTA (84.0%), showing collaborative execution feedback improves solution quality, not just best-case samples. Our results highlight execution-grounded feedback as an effective scaling mechanism for long-horizon agentic tasks.

entry.title: Vulnerability Analysis for Safe Multi-Agent Reinforcement [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2610.27293v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Safe Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (SMARL) aims to learn cooperative control policies under prescribed safety constraints. Al- though existing SMARL methods focus on enforcing safety during policy optimization, their vulnerability remains largely unexplored. This paper investigates inference-time observation attacks against SMARL, where an adversary perturbs the observations of a subset of agents, thereby altering the actions produced by their policies. We propose MinMax Attack, an attack framework that jointly selects adversarial target actions for compromised agents while accounting for the Cooperative Resistance of benign agents. We further derive a bound on the induced safety cost and characterize its relation- ship with the Compromised-Agent Budget and the Perturbation Budget. Experiments across multiple safety-critical multi-agent benchmarks and representative state-of-the-art SMARL algorithms show that MinMax Attack induces substantially higher safety costs than existing attack baselines while preserving task reward, thereby reducing its detectability and achieving both attack effectiveness and stealthiness.

entry.title: Stronger artificial intelligence breakthroughs hasten their own exhaustion [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2610.27296v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Progress in artificial intelligence is widely assumed to scale with effort: more researchers, papers and investment should accelerate discovery. Theories of technological growth instead locate the difficulty of discovery in the space of ideas. Here we show that neither scale nor space is enough: breakthroughs depend on diverse attention, which collective concentration can deplete. Across 36 years of computer science, we analyze 7.2 million papers, 73,089 peer reviews and 3.7 million researchers and their topic shifts. The field expanded while its attention narrowed sharply after the Transformer. Over half of topic-shifting researchers moved into AI, especially mid-career ones, and reviewer confidence fell by a full point on a 5-point scale. Each successive breakthrough, from AlexNet to large language models, raised the field's carrying capacity for ideas but was followed by steeper exhaustion of those ideas. Bigger breakthroughs capture attention more completely, depleting the diversity their successors may draw upon. Structural biology shows the same cycle after cryo-EM and AlphaFold. Simulations show how well-intentioned and widely used policies such as reciprocal reviewing empower prolific authors and further narrow what the field accepts. We call for institutions that protect diverse attention in artificial intelligence rather than reward concentration on the winning paradigm.

entry.title: When Does an Added Planning Capability Create Operational Value? An Observable Evidence Standard [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2610.27305v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Industrial artificial intelligence (AI) planning systems combine predictive models, optimization logic, controls, and governance rules, but improvement in the complete policy does not show whether one addition made an independent contribution or whether that contribution justifies its burden. We address this attribution problem with an observable evidence standard that separates opportunity to act, executed-plan change, operational consequence, equivalence, uncertainty, and operating scope. Using forecast-to-plan replay on Favorita, M5, and Walmart data, we apply the standard to heterogeneous planning additions. Three limits of single-indicator evaluation emerge. First, a composite policy can conceal negligible component contribution: one control changed only 15 of 681 executed plans. Second, changing execution does not guarantee stable benefit: the evaluated multi-period capability helped in several long-lead settings but was 7.6% more costly under tight capacity. Third, indirect evidence can prioritize review but cannot complete attribution. Independent runs produced different paths in 19 of 599 cases that a rule-based check predicted would be unchanged. Although a lower-cost diagnostic matched the full-evaluation winner in only 55.0% of cases, it selected an option within the $10^{-6}$ cost-equivalence tolerance in 79.5%; the remaining cases prevented the proxy from authorizing acceptance. These experiments establish capability-level contribution evidence; the organization completes the value decision by weighing it against implementation and sustaining burden. The resulting capability evidence record links the observations to validation, deployment scope, fallback, monitoring, redesign, and retirement decisions.

entry.title: Evolving Self-tuning Benchmarks for Long-Horizon Tool Use [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2610.27307v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: For AI assistants to move beyond simple chat interfaces and reliably assist users with applications like Gmail, Venmo, and Slack, we need to improve their tool-use capabilities. However, existing tool use benchmarks are still limited and difficult to scale because they rely on human supervision or are too domain-specific. To make data generation scalable, we propose, TURTLE (**T**ool **U**se **R**elated **T**asks with **L**ong-Horizon **E**volution), an Unsupervised Environment Design (UED) approach to evolve existing tasks using a proposer, a solver, and a feedback generator large language model agents. The proposer is rewarded for difficult yet solvable tasks based on the solver's empirical performance, and the feedback generator summarizes the solver's execution traces for the proposer to exploit. TURTLE produces evolving, self-tuning test suites adaptable to different environment requirements, from supporting user simulators and dense document retrieval to interacting across multiple apps. Empirical results on AppWorld, $\tau$-Bench, and AutomationBench using Gemma 4 31B-it show that the evolved tasks target the desired difficulty range (e.g., a 165\% increase in the percentage of hard tasks on AppWorld), increase task diversity (in terms of reasoning and simultaneous tool interactions), and elicit a broader range of failure modes than the original tasks.

entry.title: Unsupervised Tool Evolution for Coding Agents in Data-Lake Analytics [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2610.27327v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Coding agents can answer analytical questions over a data lake by discovering, cleaning, and joining the relevant data. However, they discard this work after each question and redo it from scratch for the next one. Tool evolution, which automatically builds and refines reusable tools across tasks, is a natural fit for this repetition. Since a ground-truth label for a data-lake question requires an expert to solve it first, we consider the unsupervised setting. We propose TEAL (Tool Evolution for Analytics over data Lakes), which evolves a library of tools and usage skills for a given Worker agent without labels. Two agents propose tools from complementary evidence, an Explorer from the data lake itself and a Critic from Worker trajectories. A proposed change is kept only if the Worker adopts the tool on a rerun without extra steps and any changed answer is supported by trajectory evidence. We also introduce TEAL-Q, which generates synthetic questions for tool evolution when real ones are unavailable. We evaluate on KramaBench and LakeQA with four Worker LLMs under step budgets, which cap the number of steps the Worker may take per question. With a tight budget of 10 or 15 steps, TEAL improves every Worker on both benchmarks, lifting Sonnet-5 at 15 steps by 9.3 points on KramaBench and 21.7 points on LakeQA. A tighter budget also yields better feedback for evolution. For example, Sonnet-5's LakeQA library evolved at 20 steps and deployed unchanged at 30 steps scores 68.3, above both the baseline (59.6) and a library evolved directly at 30 steps (64.2). Additionally, a library evolved on synthetic questions performs comparably to one evolved on real questions. These results show that useful tools can be evolved without labels, and hopefully inspire future work on what to evolve and how to obtain feedback in unsupervised agent evolution.

entry.title: Modeling Authentic Research Trajectories: A Graph View of Research Ideation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2610.27337v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The research idea in a published paper is rarely the project's initial idea. Between the two lies a closed-loop process in which researchers run experiments, derive insights, identify challenges, explore the literature, and revise the idea, with each step motivated by evidence and reasoning they can articulate. We call the path one idea takes through this process, with the evidence and reasoning behind each step, its authentic research trajectory. Although it underlies every scientific contribution, it is rarely recorded. Existing LLM-based research agents generate an idea once, refine it against reviews, literature, or their own experimental results, or search over candidate ideas and experiments. In all of them the text of the idea evolves, while the evidence and reasoning that connected one version to the next are discarded. We propose the Research Progress Graph (RPG), a representation of authentic and complete research trajectories. An RPG records the evolution of an idea as typed research states connected by cognitive transitions, each annotated with a temporal index and the reasoning behind it, which makes this evolution an explicit object of study. We ground the representation in authentic trajectories whose steps their authors justify in annotations and papers. Comparing the representations of thirty-five research agents with the RPG, we find that each is an incomplete RPG; none keeps the state that changed, the evidence that changed it, and the reasoning connecting them as one evolving record. Modeling ideation with the RPG changes how research agents should be designed, evaluated, and trained. Agents predict the next research state instead of a complete idea, ideas are evaluated as trajectories instead of final texts, and authentic trajectories serve as training data. These directions shift research agents from generating static ideas to modeling how ideas evolve.

entry.title: An LLM-Based Agent for Legal Compliance Assessment: Architecture, Memory, and Evaluation in a Canadian and Quebec Context [ * ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2610.27347v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Checking whether a text complies with a body of law is slow when done by hand and fragile when done with keyword rules. This paper presents ComplianceAgent, the legal compliance sub-agent of COMPASS, a multi-agent framework that evaluates texts along four axes: digital sovereignty, carbon impact, compliance, and ethics. The agent relies on a large language model that scores a text on a fixed rubric, grounds its judgment in a reference legal corpus, and, when the score falls at or below a critical threshold, runs a corrective chain made of self-healing rewrites, a compliance label, an explainability report, and escalation to a human reviewer. We describe what the language model does at each step, how the memory of the agent is organized, and how the same implementation can be pointed at different reference corpora. We evaluate the agent in a Canadian and Quebec context, on a corpus of thirteen legal instruments that brings together federal and provincial texts, international treaties, and municipal documents of the City of Trois-Rivi\`eres. The evaluation relies on a hand-annotated gold standard of fifteen texts and combines classification metrics, a repeated-query stability test, retrieval precision, and a composite score. On this gold standard the agent separates every conforming text from every non-conforming one, its scores remain stable under repeated queries, and the index returns relevant passages.

entry.title: REM: What to Store, When to Recall, What to Forget in Experience Memory for Coding Agents [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2610.27377v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents now autonomously complete long-horizon tasks, such as repository-level coding, through hundreds of think-act steps, yet the experience each run produces is rarely reused on the next. Prior memory systems concentrate on retrieval, finding the most relevant past trajectory. Retrieval cannot observe the running agent, so it cannot decide whether the agent needs an experience, at which point, or for how long. We introduce REM (Reusable Experience Memory), a framework that manages the memory lifecycle from inside the agent's think-act loop through three explicit decisions. What to store: each completed trajectory is consolidated into a phase-structured document, two orders of magnitude smaller than the trajectory. When to recall: the document is injected at the start of the task; the costlier implementation record is withheld until an in-loop gate detects the agent struggling. What to forget: the record is evicted after a single exposure. On repository-level bug fixing (SWE-ContextBench Lite), REM retrieves the related trajectory more accurately than every state-of-the-art memory system (68.7% vs. 55.6% match@1) and improves, in every replicate, end-task resolution (27.6% vs. 24.9%) at 17% lower cost. Injecting the same experience as a summary or raw trajectory, even when oracle-retrieved, does not. Ablating any of the three decisions reduces resolution. Altogether, these results demonstrate that the bottleneck in experience reuse is not retrieval fidelity but how experience is stored and governed across its lifecycle, opening a control-theoretic perspective on agent memory.

entry.title: Correcting Attribution Patching with a Few Exact Measurements [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2610.27393v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Mechanistic interpretability asks which language model components matter for a behavior, and activation patching answers by changing one component's activation and measuring its effect, at a cost growing with components and prompts. Attribution patching estimates these effects from one gradient pass, but its estimates can be far off, and verifying each one restores the cost. Can the structure of these errors reduce this cost? We propose Guided-AP, which uses a few exact measurements to reveal attribution patching's errors and correct unmeasured estimates. On a single prompt, many components' errors share one sign, so a small exact sample yields one correction for the rest. Over many prompts of one task, components are misestimated similarly, so a few measured prompts show what to verify and how to correct each component's average effect. Our analysis shows that choosing what to verify needs error size, while correction also needs sign. On a single prompt, the correction lowers error by up to 26% across three behaviors at the compute of verifying the largest estimates and also on larger models. Over many prompts, learned corrections cut the error of average effects on factual completion by 75% to 79%, repaying their cost in long analyses.

entry.title: When PTQ Calibration Helps or Hurts: Dose-Driven Collapse and Validation-Gated Abstention in Quantized Text Embedders [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2610.27397v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Learned post-training quantization (PTQ) calibration fits quantizer parameters on a small calibration set, and for a text embedder the natural supervision is retrieval relevance. We ask two questions that are usually conflated: how far to calibrate, and whether to calibrate at all. Across three embedders (e5-base-v2, BGE-M3, EmbeddingGemma-300m) at 4-bit weight quantization, 161 calibration runs, the outcome of a fixed procedure ranges from a gain to catastrophic degradation, and the driver is the dose of the update, measured as the functional displacement D_func of the quantized model from its uncalibrated start. On EmbeddingGemma the same learning-rate grid gives +1.47 to -71.53 points of in-domain NDCG@10 change; a label-free cosine objective collapses at the same dose (-69.52 vs -71.63), so the collapse is a property of learnable calibration rather than of retrieval supervision. Objective sensitivity is heterogeneous: on e5, ranking calibration is substantially more robust than cosine at matched displacement (+14.16 +/- 4.34 pp, 95% t-CI [+3.37, +24.96], three paired slates), whereas on BGE-M3 the ordering is directionally opposite but unresolved ([-5.18, +2.38]). Dose is the main axis but not a sufficient statistic: equal D_func reached along different paths differs by up to 1.61 pp. We therefore treat calibration as an optional intervention. A pre-registered rule that accepts a checkpoint only when a per-query paired confidence interval on a 25% calibration-validation split clears the uncalibrated baseline was run on 6 independent slates and five arms.
